sections.name: File setup (part 1)
sections.title: Settings and database connection setup
sections.what: Chooses where data is stored and builds the connection the app uses. By default it is one file in the project folder, so nothing needs to be installed.
sections.why: Lets the same code run on a laptop with SQLite and on a server with PostgreSQL, chosen by one setting.
sections.watch_out: Pointing DATABASE_URL at PostgreSQL switches several behaviors at once, including pool sizes, so check the related settings together.

sections.name: File setup (part 2)
sections.title: Base class for table definitions
sections.what: Creates the parent class that every table definition must inherit from, so the app can find all tables when it builds them.
sections.why: Likely reason: SQLAlchemy needs one shared base that tracks every table. No further reason is stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: A model that does not inherit from this base will never be created by the table-building step.

sections.name: get_db
sections.title: Per-request database session
sections.what: Gives each web request its own database session and closes it when the request finishes, even if an error happened.
sections.why: Keeps requests from sharing one working space and makes sure connections are not left open.
sections.watch_out: Autocommit is off, so changes made in a route are lost unless the route calls commit.

sections.name: init_db
sections.title: Create all tables
sections.what: Creates every table defined in the models if it does not exist yet. It loads the full model list first so none are missed.
sections.why: The docstring says to use Alembic migrations in production, so this is a shortcut for development and setup.
sections.watch_out: A new model must be added to the import list here, or its table will be silently skipped.

sections.name: check_and_init_db
sections.title: Startup check that builds missing tables
sections.what: On startup, looks for the projects table and builds all tables if it is missing. If the check itself fails, it tries the full build instead.
sections.why: Makes the database ready without a special development flag, as the docstring says.
sections.watch_out: Only the projects table is checked, so a database that has projects but lacks other tables will not be repaired.

sections.name: test_connection
sections.title: Connection test used at startup and by health check
sections.what: Runs a trivial query to confirm the database answers, logs the result, and returns true or false. The health check endpoint also depends on it.
sections.why: Lets the app stop early at startup if the database is unreachable, and lets the health endpoint report status on demand.
sections.watch_out: Because the health endpoint calls this on every request, frequent polling runs a query and writes a log line each time.

sections.name: receive_connect
sections.title: Logs each new connection
sections.what: Writes a log entry each time a new database connection opens, noting which database type is in use.
sections.why: Likely reason: helps trace connection activity when debugging. No further reason is stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: This is a second listener on the same connection event as the SQLite settings, so both run on every new connection and may add log noise.

sections.name: receive_close
sections.title: Logs each closed connection
sections.what: Writes a log entry when a database connection closes.
sections.why: Likely reason: the same debugging purpose as the open log.
sections.watch_out: No log level filter is set in the visible code, so these entries may appear in normal logs.

summary: Connects the app to its database, creates missing tables on startup, and gives each web request its own database session.
purpose: Gives the rest of the app one shared place to connect to the database. It uses a single SQLite file by default and switches to PostgreSQL when a DATABASE_URL setting is given.
why: Likely reason: keeps database setup in one file so other parts of the app do not each configure it. The SQLite default lets the app run on locked-down computers without installing a database server, as the file header states.
how: 1. Reads the DATABASE_URL setting, or builds a default SQLite file path in the project root. 2. Creates the connection engine with settings that differ for SQLite and PostgreSQL. 3. Registers SQLite safety settings that run each time a connection opens. 4. On startup, the test_connection and check_and_init_db functions confirm the database answers and create missing tables. 5. The get_db function gives each request a session and closes it when the request ends.
inputs: Environment settings DATABASE_URL, DB_ECHO, DB_POOL_SIZE and DB_MAX_OVERFLOW. Table definitions from the models package.
outputs: A database engine, a session factory, a base class for table definitions, and the get_db function. Writes the solar_benchmarking.db file when SQLite is used. Writes log lines about connections and table creation.
risks: Table creation only checks whether a table named projects exists, so a partly built database can be skipped. Setting DB_ECHO to true floods logs with every SQL statement. The health check runs a connection test on every call. Any model not listed in the import list will not get a table.
debug: If the app will not start, look for database_connection_test or database_connection_failed in the logs, then confirm DATABASE_URL and that the folder holding the database file is writable. If a table is missing, check that its model appears in the import list inside init_db. If you see extra files named with -wal or -shm next to the database, that is normal for SQLite WAL mode.
